---
title: "Tech Value: performance per dollar"
subtitle: "US retail prices against open benchmark scores, for desktop CPUs and graphics cards"
---

```{python}
from IPython.display import Markdown
from itables import init_notebook_mode, show

from pdi import site
from pdi.tech_value import dashboard

# Bundle the table script into the page instead of loading it from a CDN.
init_notebook_mode(connected=False)

value, meta = site.load("tech-value", "value")
history, hist_meta = site.load("tech-value", "price_history")
coverage, cov_meta = site.load("tech-value", "coverage")
bench, bench_meta = site.load("tech-value", "benchmarks")
version = meta.get("blender_version")

COLUMNS = {
    "model_key": "Model",
    "score_per_dollar": "Score per $",
    "price_usd": "Lowest price (USD)",
    "Retailer": "Cheapest at",
    "median_price_usd": "Median price (USD)",
    "n_retailers": "Stores",
    "Confidence": "Confidence",
    "collected_date": "Price collected",
    "score": "Benchmark score",
    "n_runs": "Benchmark runs",
    "backend": "Backend",
    "n_listings": "Listings",
}
COLUMNS = {
    k: v for k, v in COLUMNS.items()
    if k == "Retailer" or k in value.columns or (k == "Confidence" and "confidence" in value.columns)
}
CONFIDENCE = {"low": "Low: single listing", "normal": "Normal"}


def ranking(kind: str, label: str):
    part = value[value["kind"] == kind] if len(value) else value
    if part.empty:
        return Markdown(site.empty_state(meta, label))
    names = {m["id"]: m["name"] for m in meta.get("sources", [])}
    part = part.assign(Retailer=[
        f'<a href="{url}">{names.get(key, key)}</a>' if url else names.get(key, key)
        for key, url in zip(part["retailer"], part["listing_url"])
    ])
    if "confidence" in part.columns:
        part = part.assign(Confidence=part["confidence"].map(CONFIDENCE))
    table = part[list(COLUMNS)].rename(columns=COLUMNS).round(
        {"Score per $": 3, "Benchmark score": 1}
    )
    return show(table, paging=True, pageLength=25, order=[[1, "desc"]], showIndex=False,
                classes="display compact", allow_html=True)
```

The charts below rank every model that has both a fresh price and a Blender benchmark score.
They share one set of filters and one selected model: pick a model in the list, or click any
dot or bar, and every chart follows it. Graphics cards and CPUs are never compared with each other.

## Performance vs price

*How much performance am I getting for the money?* Each dot is one model: its lowest new
listing against its Blender score. Up and to the left is better. Prices are on a log scale by
default, so a step to the right is the same percentage increase anywhere on the axis. The dotted lines are the
median price and median score of the models in view, so the top-left corner (tinted) holds the
cheap, fast models and the bottom-right the expensive, slow ones. The fastest model is rarely
the best value: compare the two labelled dots. Hollow dots have a price from a single listing.
With the frontier switched on, faded dots are dominated (see the efficiency frontier below).
Graphics card scores come from each maker's own Blender backend (OptiX for NVIDIA, HIP for AMD,
oneAPI for Intel), which favours NVIDIA cards; the backend is shown when you hover a dot.

## Performance per dollar leaderboard

*Which model gives the most performance for every dollar?* Blender score divided by the lowest
new listing, in benchmark points per US dollar. This is a ratio, not a percentage: 8.0 means
eight points of score for each dollar of price. The price is the same lowest listing the
tables below use.

## Price premium vs performance gain

*Is the more expensive model worth it?* Every other model in view, placed by how much more (or
less) it costs and how much faster (or slower) it is than the baseline, which is the selected
model (the diamond at 0, 0). On the dashed line, price and performance rise in proportion.
Above it, the extra performance outpaces the extra cost; below it, you pay more than you gain.

## Performance distribution

*Where does the selected model sit against the rest?* Benchmark scores of the ranked models in
view, with the 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentiles. The comparison set is only the models
this site can price, so "faster than 90%" means 90% of this set, not of all hardware.
Percentiles are not drawn for fewer than ten models.

## Efficiency frontier

*Which models are dominated by a better alternative?* A model is dominated when another model in
view costs no more and scores at least as high, and is strictly better on one of the two. The
frontier is the set no model dominates; it is the dashed line on the performance vs price chart.
It is worked out separately for graphics cards and CPUs, and again whenever the filters change.

```{python}
#| output: asis
html('<div id="vd-frontier-out"></div>')
```

A comparison by hardware generation is not shown: the data has no structured generation field,
and guessing generations from model names is not reliable enough to publish.

## Price history

*Are prices rising, falling or flat?* The lowest new, online-available listing per model on each
day the collector ran. Daily prices cannot be backfilled, so the history only goes back to the day
the collector was switched on. No trend is stated until the history spans
`{python} dashboard.MIN_HISTORY_DAYS` days.

## Data coverage and freshness

How many models make it from a benchmark score to a ranked price. The price collectors look up
the `{python} dashboard.config.CRAWLER_MODELS_PER_KIND` most-benchmarked models of each kind every
day; a model is ranked only when a listing is recognised as that model and its price is no more
than `{python} dashboard.config.PRICE_MAX_AGE_DAYS` days old.

```{python}
#| output: asis
html(dashboard.coverage_html(bench, value, history))
html(f"""
<script>window.__vdDefine = window.define; window.define = undefined;</script>
<script src="{plotly_src}" charset="utf-8"></script>
<script>window.define = window.__vdDefine;</script>
<script>{js}</script>
""")
```

## Ranking tables

**Score per dollar** is the median [Blender benchmark](https://opendata.blender.org/) score of
a part divided by its cheapest new listing among the US retailers collected. It measures rendering throughput
per dollar and nothing else: not gaming frame rates, not power draw, not noise. Treat a high
value as a reason to look closer, not as a recommendation.

Every price is shown with the retailer it came from and the date this site collected it.
Prices come from one store that allows automated collection and, once a week, from Amazon US
and Best Buy listings supplied by a data provider. Only Amazon listings sold by Amazon.com or
the part's own brand, and Best Buy listings sold by Best Buy itself, are counted, so every
price is for a new part. A cheaper listing may exist elsewhere.

A row marked **Low: single listing** has only one listing behind its price. That is often a
marketplace seller's asking price for a part that is no longer made, so treat its score per
dollar as unreliable. Type "Normal" in the search box to hide those rows.

```{python}

```

## Listing coverage

How much of what is on sale could be matched. A listing has to be recognised as a specific
model, and that model needs enough benchmark runs on the Blender version in use. Unmatched
products are left out of the ranking, never guessed.

```{python}
if coverage.empty:
    display(Markdown(site.empty_state(cov_meta, "Coverage")))
else:
    display(Markdown(coverage.rename(columns={
        "kind": "Kind", "listings": "Listings collected",
        "listings_recognised": "Recognised as a model", "models_priced": "Distinct models priced",
        "models_with_score": "Models with a benchmark score", "share_with_score": "Share with score",
    }).to_markdown(index=False, floatfmt=".0%")))
```

All recognised models with enough benchmark runs, whether or not a price has been collected.
